title: Mark June Dairy Month with Industry-Wide Reform
author: Anthony Pahnke
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/06/IMG_0105-680x532.jpeg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/06/18/mark-
june-dairy-month-with-industry-wide-reform/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/06/IMG_0105-680x532.jpeg)

Barn at small dairy on the French Prairie in Oregon's Willamette Valley.
Photo: Jeffrey St. Clair.

Sometimes the truth stares you right in the face.

Case in point – in the middle of his [agricultural roundtable
event](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jtJeBu0eEvo) with farmers and
Republican representatives held this past June 5th in Chippewa Falls,
Wisconsin, President Trump took a moment to reflect about a different meeting
he once had with another group of producers. As the President remembered, he
told the farmers, “I’m going to get you a subsidy.” To his surprise they
responded that they didn’t want subsidies, but rather, “a level playing
field.”

It would be easy to gloss over the truth in Trump’s recollection, especially
as he rambled on about many things unrelated to farming such as repairing
monuments around Washington DC, his disdain for Democrats, and how the
Southern border was closed to migrants. This, as NFL Hall of Famer, Joe
Thomas, sat to Trump’s side and [drew gushing
remarks](https://madison.com/news/state-regional/government-
politics/article_94391011-755c-52e0-bad7-cd9289c8ca56.html) from the President
about the retired player’s body.

[Unlike Thomas](https://www.spotrac.com/nfl/player/_/id/2348/joe-thomas), most
farmers cannot draw on millions to stay on the land. Instead, they can turn to
the government to promote fair markets. As much could happen now, during June
Dairy Month, as the Farm Bill is working through Congress and much needed
relief could come by including in the ominous piece of legislation key reforms
to the dairy industry.

To be fair, discussion during Trump’s roundtable did include some dairy
policies.

Secretary Rollins, for instance, alluded to trade deals that would increase
exports. Representative Derrick Van Orden, whose district the roundtable took
place in and who appears in [trouble of losing his
seat](https://www.wispolitics.com/2026/cooke-campaign-new-poll-rebecca-cooke-
grows-lead-over-derrick-van-orden-to-50-46-in-closely-watched-house-race/) to
the daughter of dairy farmers, Rebecca Cooke, touted the [Whole Milk for
Healthy Kids Act](https://www.usda.gov/about-usda/news/press-
releases/2026/05/08/usda-implements-president-trumps-whole-milk-healthy-kids-
act). The Act restores whole and reduced fat (2%) milk options at schools.

The problem is that both initiatives don’t do much.

First, the evidence shows that increasing exports doesn’t keep people farming.

[Farm Bureau data](https://www.fb.org/market-intel/strong-start-fragile-
future-u-s-dairys-trade-balancing-act) shows that since 2016, total dairy
export value has doubled from just over $4 million to over $8 in 2024. But
during this same period, the number of licensed dairy herds has collapsed,
[from over 40,000, to under 25,000](https://www.ers.usda.gov/data-
products/chart-gallery/113820).

Meanwhile, serving milk at school lunch does open markets. And nationwide,
[since 2024](https://thehustle.co/originals/why-everybodys-drinking-milk-
again), more people have been consuming milk after years of decline. But even
amid rising demand, in 2025 Wisconsin saw a [700% increase in
bankruptcies](https://www.fb.org/market-intel/farm-bankruptcies-continued-to-
climb-in-2025), particularly hitting dairy farmers.

Instead of such piecemeal fixes, the dairy industry needs industry-wide
reform, as the farmers who spoke with Trump once said, “to level the playing
field.”

The proposal that would advance such change is the [Milk from Family Dairies
Act (MFDA](https://nffc.net/what-we-do/dairy/)). Created by the National
Family Farm Coalition and endorsed by [over 90
organizations](https://nffc.net/national-call-for-fair-prices-systemic-dairy-
policy-reform/), the MFDA ensures farmers a decent price without driving up
costs for consumers and relying on taxpayer-funded subsidies.

The principle behind the MFDA is supply management, [similar to the system in
Canada](https://www.nfu.ca/learn/supply-management/). In this system, consumer
supply demands are balanced with prices that farmers are paid for their milk
in regular meetings of stakeholders. For farmers, receiving compensation for
at least the cost of production is a big deal, as since 2021, even taking into
consideration advantages of increasing herd size, dairy producers across the
board have consistently had [to sell their milk at a
loss](https://www.ers.usda.gov/amber-waves/2026/february/fewer-farms-more-
milk-the-changing-structure-and-costs-of-us-dairy-farming) as the price of
feed, seed, and fertilizer rise.

Consumers benefit as the MFDA makes investments in local dairy processors,
increasing competition to drive down prices, and corporate concentration in
the industry is targeted with anti-trust enforcement [to curtail price gouging
by large-scale
retailers](https://www.ams.usda.gov/sites/default/files/media/USDAPlan_EO_COMPETITION.pdf)
at the grocery store. Currently, taxpayers pick up the tab for farmers who
have financial troubles with subsidies, or direct payments, which Trump has
[handed out repeatedly](https://www.ewg.org/news-insights/news-
release/2025/12/bridge-nowhere-trump-bailout-again-flow-largest-wealthiest-
farms) across his administrations.

Unlike Joe Thomas, most farmers don’t have millions to keep them going.
Instead, they have the government, which should ensure fair markets. So, to
mark June Dairy month, our lawmakers should listen to farmers, level the
playing field, and include elements from the MFDA into the Farm Bill.
